lessons.title: Case Study: Building a Simple Risk Parity Portfolio With Nifty, G-Secs, and Gold

children.text: The last lesson gave you the math. This one turns it into a portfolio you could actually place orders for tomorrow: which instruments to buy, how to pull the data, how to handle the fact that your volatility estimate depends on the lookback window you pick, and how to translate a set of decimal weights into rupee amounts and fund units.

A minimal Indian risk parity portfolio needs three return drivers that do not all move together for the same reason: growth-sensitive equity, interest-rate-sensitive government debt, and a store of value that tends to hold up when both of the other two wobble.

body.caption: The three sleeves, what each one is doing in the portfolio, and typical access route

cells: Broad exposure to Indian equity growth, the most volatile and highest long-run expected return sleeve
A Nifty 50 index fund or ETF, such as Nippon India ETF Nifty BeES (NIFTYBEES)
Interest-rate duration risk, a return driver largely independent of corporate earnings and, in stress periods, often negatively correlated with equity
A long-duration gilt or G-Sec index fund/ETF; several AMCs including SBI, ICICI Prudential, and Nippon India offer gilt fund options with duration close to a 10-year benchmark
A store-of-value asset with a historically low or mildly positive correlation to Indian equity, and a different set of drivers again (global real rates, currency, central bank demand)
A gold ETF such as Nippon India ETF Gold BeES (GOLDBEES), or Sovereign Gold Bonds if you are comfortable with their lock-in
~0.40% to 0.80% (ETF); no expense ratio, but a spread, for physical gold

body.text: Fund names above are named for illustration of the category (equity index, gilt/G-Sec, gold ETF), not a recommendation. Expense ratios, exact fund availability, and specific gilt fund duration profiles change over time. Check the current factsheet and duration of any fund before using it, particularly the gilt fund, since a gilt fund's tenor may not track a pure 10-year G-Sec exactly.

children.text: You need a daily price history for all three sleeves, ideally the ETF or index fund's own NAV rather than the underlying benchmark, since NAVs bake in tracking error and, for the equity leg, dividend reinvestment. NSE's bhavcopy archives and AMFI's daily NAV files cover Indian mutual funds and ETFs going back years, and Zerodha's Kite Connect historical data API is a convenient way to pull daily closes programmatically if you already trade through Zerodha. For gold, use the ETF's own NAV rather than the international spot price, since the ETF NAV already reflects INR conversion, import duty, and GST embedded in domestic gold pricing.
Step 2: Choosing a Lookback Window, and Why It Matters

Volatility and correlation are not fixed numbers, they are estimates over whatever window of history you choose, and different windows give different answers. Using the same correlation structure as the last lesson (-0.10 equity-debt, 0.05 equity-gold, 0.00 debt-gold) but three different illustrative volatility estimates, one drawn from a more recent, choppier 1-year window and two from calmer, longer 3-year and 5-year windows, produces three slightly different risk parity solutions.

body.caption: Illustrative ERC weights and portfolio volatility under three different lookback windows

body.text: Compare this to chapter 1: a 50 basis point nudge to one return assumption threw a mean-variance optimizer's weights into a completely different portfolio. Here, moving between a 1-year and a 5-year volatility lookback, a much bigger change in input than 50 basis points, shifts each sleeve's weight by only about 1 to 2 percentage points. This is risk parity's stability advantage from chapter 1 showing up directly: because the optimization never touches expected returns, it inherits none of that estimation-error amplification.

children.text: That said, the choice is not free of consequences, notice the portfolio's overall volatility estimate ranges from 4.31% to 5.50% depending on the window, a meaningfully wide range for something you might be sizing leverage against later in this course. Chapter 4 covers the pitfalls of lookback window selection in far more depth. For this build, use a 3-year daily window as the working default, long enough to smooth out short-term noise, short enough to still reflect the current market regime reasonably well.
Using the 3-year window as the base case, the risk parity solver from the last lesson, Spinu's convex formulation, gives the following weights.
Step 4: Translating Weights Into a Real Portfolio

Take a Rs 10 lakh corpus and apply the 20.1% / 57.6% / 22.2% split. The NAVs below are illustrative snapshots purely for the arithmetic, always use the current NAV on the day you actually place an order.

body.caption: Illustrative Rs 10,00,000 risk parity portfolio, 3-year window weights (percentages rounded to one decimal, so amounts sum to Rs 9,99,000, with the remaining Rs 1,000 left as rounding-residual cash)

body.text: More than half the corpus, 57.6%, sits in the gilt fund. That can feel wrong to an investor used to thinking in capital terms, where a 'serious' portfolio is supposed to be equity-heavy. It is correct in risk terms, which is the entire point of everything covered so far in this course. Explaining that distinction clearly is as much a part of running a risk parity strategy as computing it.

children.text: Step 5: When to Rebalance, a Preview

Prices move every day, so the moment you place these orders, the actual capital weights start drifting away from the 20.1/57.6/22.3 target, and updated volatility and correlation estimates will nudge the target itself over time. Two common triggers decide when to trade back toward target.

columns.label: Calendar rebalancing
points: Rebalance on a fixed schedule, e.g. quarterly or monthly
Simple to implement and to explain to a client or committee
Can rebalance when nothing meaningful has actually drifted, generating unnecessary transaction costs

columns.label: Threshold rebalancing
points: Rebalance only when a sleeve's actual risk contribution drifts beyond a set band, e.g. more than 5 percentage points from its 33.3% target
Trades only when it matters, generally lower turnover
Needs the risk contribution to be monitored continuously, not just checked on a fixed date

children.text: This course comes back to rebalancing in much more depth in chapter 4, including the specific mistakes that quietly inflate a risk parity backtest's returns. For now, the takeaway is simpler: decide your rebalancing rule before you place the first order, not after you see how the sleeves have drifted.

body.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize  # pip install scipy

def solve_erc(vol, corr, n_iter_bounds=1e-6):
    cov = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr
    n = len(vol)

    def objective(w):
        return 0.5 * w @ cov @ w - (1 / n) * np.sum(np.log(w))

    result = minimize(
        objective,
        x0=np.full(n, 1 / n),
        method='SLSQP',
        bounds=[(n_iter_bounds, None)] * n,
    )
    w = result.x / result.x.sum()
    port_vol = np.sqrt(w @ cov @ w)
    return w, port_vol

def allocate(corpus_rupees, weights, navs):
    amounts = corpus_rupees * weights
    units = amounts / navs
    return amounts, units

# Replace with your own 3-year daily NAV series based vol/corr estimates
vol = np.array([0.14, 0.05, 0.12])          # Nifty 50, Gilt fund, Gold ETF
corr = np.array([
    [1.00, -0.10, 0.05],
    [-0.10, 1.00, 0.00],
    [0.05, 0.00, 1.00],
])

weights, port_vol = solve_erc(vol, corr)
print('ERC weights:', np.round(weights * 100, 1), '%')
print('Portfolio volatility:', f'{port_vol:.2%}')

corpus = 1_000_000  # Rs 10 lakh
navs = np.array([245.0, 22.0, 68.0])  # illustrative, use current NAVs on order day
amounts, units = allocate(corpus, weights, navs)
for label, amt, u in zip(['Nifty 50 ETF', 'Gilt fund', 'Gold ETF'], amounts, units):
    print(f'{label}: Rs {amt:,.0f}  (~{u:,.0f} units)')
body.caption: This script chains together everything in this lesson: solve for ERC weights, then convert them into rupee amounts and approximate fund units for a given corpus. Swap in real NAV histories and current NAVs before using it to place actual orders.

body.title: Six Months Later
body.scenario: Six months after you build the Rs 10 lakh portfolio above, Nifty 50 has rallied sharply while the gilt fund has been roughly flat and gold has drifted down slightly. You check the portfolio and find the equity sleeve's risk contribution has risen to about 41% of total portfolio risk, well above its 33.3% target, while debt has fallen to about 27%.
body.prompt: Using the threshold rebalancing rule described in this lesson (rebalance if a sleeve's risk contribution drifts more than 5 percentage points from its 33.3% target), would you rebalance here, and in which direction would the trade go?
body.modelAnswer: Yes. Equity's risk contribution at roughly 41% is about 8 percentage points above its 33.3% target, comfortably past the 5-point threshold, and debt's roughly 27% is about 6 points below target, also past the threshold. The trade would sell part of the equity sleeve, which has grown both in rupee terms and in risk contribution after the rally, and buy more of the gilt sleeve, bringing both sleeves' risk contributions back toward 33.3%. This is the mechanical, non-discretionary version of 'sell high, buy low' that a risk parity rebalancing rule produces automatically.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In the Rs 10 lakh case study, why does the gilt (G-Sec) sleeve receive the largest rupee allocation, 57.6%, even though it is expected to be the lowest-returning of the three sleeves over the long run?
options: Because gilt funds have the lowest expense ratios of the three instruments

Because risk parity allocates capital to equalize risk contribution, not expected return, and the gilt sleeve's low volatility means it needs a much larger rupee weight to contribute an equal share of portfolio risk
Because SEBI mandates a minimum debt allocation for retail portfolios
Because the gilt fund had the best historical return over the lookback window used
body.explanation: Nothing about expected return enters a risk parity calculation. The gilt sleeve's volatility is roughly a third of equity's, so achieving an equal risk contribution requires giving it a correspondingly larger capital weight. A large rupee allocation to the lowest-volatility sleeve is the entire mechanism of risk parity, not a side effect.

body.text: Building a real risk parity portfolio is mostly a data and process problem layered on top of the math from the last lesson: pick sleeves with genuinely different return drivers, choose a lookback window deliberately, solve for ERC weights, and decide your rebalancing rule before, not after, you place the first order. The resulting portfolio will look capital-heavy in debt to anyone thinking in rupee terms. That is exactly what a risk-balanced portfolio is supposed to look like.

points: A minimal Indian risk parity portfolio needs three return drivers that do not all respond to the same shocks: Nifty 50 equity, 10-year G-Sec duration, and gold.

Volatility and correlation estimates depend on the lookback window chosen. Moving between a 1-year and 5-year window shifted this case study's weights by only 1 to 2 percentage points per sleeve, a far smaller swing than the mean-variance instability from chapter 1, but portfolio volatility estimates still ranged from 4.31% to 5.50% across windows.
On a 3-year window, the illustrative ERC solution was roughly 20.1% equity, 57.6% gilt/G-Sec, and 22.2% gold, each contributing exactly 33.3% of portfolio risk.
A large rupee weight in the lowest-volatility sleeve is not a mistake, it is the mechanism. Debt receiving the biggest allocation in this example reflects risk balance, not a return forecast.

Decide a rebalancing rule, calendar-based or threshold-based, before placing the first order. Chapter 4 covers the common mistakes that show up when this decision is made carelessly or after the fact.
